newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian inflation seen rising in first quarter.
newsitem.headline: Indian inflation seen rising in first quarter.

text.p: Indian inflation, which surpassed 7.5 percent last month, is set to rise further in the first quarter of 1997 fuelled by a growing money supply and higher production costs, some analysts said on Monday.
"I see inflation around nine percent by the end of March," said Amit Rajpal, banking analyst at Prime Broking. "It will be double-digit within six months."

Year-on-year inflation, measured by the wholesale price index, was at a 56-week high of 7.58 percent on December 21 against 7.08 percent the previous week and 6.0 percent a year earlier, according to the Industry Ministry.
Rajpal said an easing of monetary policy by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had contributed to the build-up of inflationary pressures.
The RBI has cut the banks' cash reserve ratio requirements to 10.5 percent (effective January 4, 1997) from 14 percent in April 1996 in response to industry complaints of a liquidity crunch.
It will be cut again, to 10 percent, on January 18.
Monetary supply growth was within set targets but economic growth had been below projections, Rajpal said.
"You set targets for M3 (money supply) based on a certain projected output. Now this year, while M3 growth has been within target, economic growth has been slower than expected," he said.

"Basically the RBI has opened monetary floodgates in an attempt to stimulate growth," Rajpal said. "But there has been no pick-up in demand... All this money is just floating around stoking inflationary pressures."

Madan Sabnavis, economist with term lending institution Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India (ICICI), said inflation was set to rise but he did not feel that monetary policy was responsible.
"The economy is in the first stage of a recession," he said. "Excess money leads to inflation only if there is demand. This is not the case at present."

He predicted 10 percent inflation by the end of March more on account of cost-push factors such as last year's increase in railway freight and petroleum product prices which would increase production costs.
"The emphasis this year has been on stimulating growth whereas last year it was on containing inflation," he said. "I do not see monetary policy having much impact on inflation."

Anindya Chatterjee, analyst at Natwest Markets, said inflation seemed to have bottomed out and would be on the upswing in coming months although he put the end-March inflation figure lower, at 8.0-8.5 percent.

"The current rise in inflation has been largely on account of a rise in prices of primary articles," he said. "But agricultural production is expected to be good this year. That should help keep prices of primary articles in check and contain inflation."
